utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We have received word that Mr. Wladimiroff will not be here through to the 9th, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That is right, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Very good. I understand there was a problem this morning in bringing Mr. Tadic. I do not know what the delay was, but we have been here waiting. If there is anything that we can do, Mr. Kay, please let me know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. We are unaware of what happened as yet, only receiving information through the Registry. That is all.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. As the court will recall, Mr. Gutic was on the stand when we adjourned on Thursday. MR. VASIF GUTIC, recalled

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gutic, you will understand that you are still under oath, do you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware of that.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER CONTINUED
utterances.text: Sir, I would like to begin with a point of clarification. When you were testifying on Thursday you mentioned the expression "ici na kupanje" which was interpreted back to us as "to take a swim". Does that expression mean to take a swim such as in a swimming pool or does it mean to take a bath as when someone cleans themselves in a bath tub?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, given that there was not enough water in the camp, in the beginning people were allowed to the neighbouring the houses so that they would take a shower or take a bath, but then that was later used as an expression for being able to leave the camp for a while. It meant to go search for food, apart from going for hygienic reasons and, as you put it, not to swim, more to take a bath.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER CONTINUED
utterances.text: When prisoners left the camp briefly for such purposes, were they required to leave some form of identification such as their licna karta, their identification card, with camp authorities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That was the only possible way to leave. Everybody was leaving licna karta at the checkpoint, and then they would have to be back to report at the point, checkpoint, and pick up their licna card, their ID. Then they would be searched to see what they brought in. It was controlled on the part of the soldiers who were manning that checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER CONTINUED
utterances.text: As I recall, when we adjourned on Thursday, you were discussing the time when you were taken to the Crisis Staff in Prijedor where camp Commander Kuruzovic and deputy Commander Puhalic and the Balaban twins were. I believe you mentioned that you were taken back by Major Kuruzovic in his vehicle and that he talked a bit on the way back. On the way back to Trnopolje camp from the Crisis Staff, did you see tractors and trailers loaded with furniture and other goods?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, during our drive towards Trnopolje, we passed checkpoints, Serbian Army checkpoints, and there were Serb tractors who were collecting all the valuables, the furniture, that they would find in Muslim houses, and at one point the Major said that, "This is not how you create a state, how you create a country". He said it pretty strictly and then he remembered how we were here as well. Then he explained he was talking to the soldier who was escorting us, that at that time ones are getting rich by looting these houses, that they are sitting at these checkpoints while other soldiers are fighting in the front line, that in some way that was not right. I do not know if that is what he -- that if he said it because we were there or he had his own reasons, but that is how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER CONTINUED
utterances.text: Sir, on Thursday you discussed beatings and killings in Trnopolje camp. Were there also rapes at Trnopolje camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, unlike Keraterm or Omarska, in Trnopolje the large majority of people consisted of women and children and, unfortunately, women were being taken out by the Serb military and, unfortunately, they were raped during that period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER CONTINUED
utterances.text: Were the women prisoners in Trnopolje or in the surrounding area raped under different circumstances? Were there different categories of circumstances in which these rapes occurred?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry. Yes, given the place, so to speak, of where the rapes occurred, the girls were taken either outside of the camp, from the rooms in the camp to the houses surrounding the camp, in the vicinity of the camp, or usually the perpetrators were the guards who were guarding the camp, or they were taken to the houses which were farther away from the camp. A third category, I would say, are the girls and women who were in the houses who have in a way been released from the camps to the villages, and from those houses were also taken away and raped.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER CONTINUED
utterances.text: How old was the youngest female you treated for rape or for the aftermath of the rape?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The youngest young girl that I spoke to after that terrible act was 12 and a half years old, and I still remember to date that case which was truly terrifying. It was a girl who was still a child and, as she said, she did not have her first period at the time. She asked -- the night before that, the afternoon, I met that girl in the clinic. She brought her old grandmother to be checked and I talked to her, and the next day after that rape she wanted to talk to me because she knew me, she trusted me. Her mother came to the clinic and this terrible act had occurred, and I agreed to go there because she did not want to come out. She could not. She did not have the strength. So I went to that room which was in a way isolated. I saw her in the corner. She did not register anything around her. So she had that dejected look, she was staring in front of her, sort of, expressionless stare. There was nothing in it. That left a terrible impression on me because I met her the night before. I saw her eyes, those beautiful eyes, and they were gone. I tried to open her up, to help her, to sort of force her to talk so that it would bring some relief because, if I managed to do it, if I succeeded in that, it would save her life because she would not hate all men later. After about an hour of my attempts, I succeeded. She started to talk, to talk, to talk, everything, from the first moment to the last. She was terribly -- that kind of perversion at the way she was raped is just terrible, but she told the entire story and she started crying terribly. Unfortunately, beside that, we could not do much for her. We gave her some painkillers and that day she was deported. I do not know anything about her fate thereafter.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER CONTINUED
utterances.text: Sir, how old or young was the youngest victim of rape whom you heard about from guards?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, one day one of the guards came up to us who was often at the Trnopolje camp, and he was injured. He asked for medical help. His right arm was hurt by chards of glass, so we needed to disinfect it and wrap it. So then during the conversation here we asked what happened. He said that he had, as he called it, an intervention. I said, I asked what kind. He said that he was at Suhi Brod, that a woman had reported the disappearance of her two daughters at the checkpoint in Kozarac and that they called him up and that he went to intervene and, with his colleagues, he forcibly entered that house and arrested one of the soldiers who, as he said, was playing with two girls who were nude. They were without any clothes. One was 11 and the other one was 12. He said that he was just playing with them, that he was not doing anything, and we could not have known.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER CONTINUED
utterances.text: Were women from Trnopolje subjected to group or gang rapes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Unfortunately, those things also occurred. Women who were taken, who were supposed to be deported in trains or buses or trucks would be separated from men in those rooms, and they were taken away to these group rapes. But I talked to one of the victims who was subjected to rapes by several men. She said that that night she was raped by seven men. Only in the morning she was able to escape from them and to return to the camp in the early morning hours. She was asking for our help because she had terrible pains and she was haemorrhaging and we helped her as much as we could.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER CONTINUED
utterances.text: What was her age or approximate age?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: She was 19 and she had a small baby, a six-month old baby.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER CONTINUED
utterances.text: Were women taken in groups from Trnopolje camp to be raped?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were taken sometimes in groups. In Trnopolje camp, it was, what was well known was the so-called night of the tank squad. A group of soldiers came late, around 11 p.m., in some kind of a truck. They entered the movie theatre which was within the camp where these girls and women were located. According to our information, eight to 10 women were taken out that night, and two men who were there, who found themselves there, were beaten by iron bars. We treated one of them and we sent him to Prijedor and then he later came back. He lost an eye as a result of the beating. That night, around 2 o'clock in the morning, after midnight, they returned these women, that group, but from another room they took several others and took them with them. Naturally, all the cases are not known to us. They hid it, the women did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER CONTINUED
utterances.text: Actually, I wanted to ask you about that. Is it possible to estimate with any accuracy the number of rapes which occurred in Trnopolje or the surrounding areas based on the people you treated or the reports you have received?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Unfortunately, it is difficult to give such estimates. Rape as an act in our region, this is a patriarchal environment and it is a terrible act, so that these victims attempted to hide these as much as they could. Very often, mothers or sisters of girls who would come to us to help them, when we asked them to come and talk to us so that we could see them, they said that they could not because they were threatened that they would be killed if they report this to anyone, to us or others. So that very often we were powerless to do anything more. It is hard to say, but they were very frequent, very, very frequent. Most frequently, the attempts were made to hide the fact within the circle of the family or the ones who were present at the time when they were taken away, so it was not talked about.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER CONTINUED
utterances.text: Of the categories of potential victims you mentioned earlier, was one group more vulnerable to the risk or likelihood of rape than the others?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, very often, most often, so to speak, those young girls, 16, 17, 18, 19 years of age, simply they were beautiful and young and so that was, I guess, part of the pleasure. Apart from the age, they also were taking women who were placed in the rooms of either the store or the big hall where they were separated from men, where they were, those who were in the school. Because there were men there, soldiers did not dare go in there as much because they feared reactions of men, however much fear there was, but there was a real possibility that these men would react, that they would protect their sisters or mothers or acquaintances. So that given the location where they were, that played a part. Also, those who were threatened were the girls who were coming bringing food to their brothers or friends. That was our only source of food supply for a while. There was a great hunger at the camp so they had to travel a very dangerous road, several kilometres through the fields or small by-roads. Often times they were accosted there and raped.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Can I intervene? The witness mentioned the hall, the large hall, is that the same building as the picture theatre we have heard of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that was a hall where that was before a theatre, a movie theatre house, before the war. That is where they were -- the women were put who were prepared, so to speak, for deportation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What about the women in the areas adjacent to you or surrounding Trnopolje camp from which men had already been cleansed? What was their risk factor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For them also there was an enormous risk, because soldiers knew that there were no men there, that all the men were somewhere in camps, so that they could freely come there, move through those villages, enter the houses during the day. They were taking pieces of furniture or electric appliances or such, and at the same time they were observing these girls. Then, usually towards the evening, at dusk, they would come for these girls. They would walk in. They would take the girls that they liked and they were taking them away to some houses of their own usually. There were several houses where those rapes most frequently occurred -- the abandoned Muslim houses that were a bit outside of the village where the Muslim population still lived.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER CONTINUED
utterances.text: Were some of the rapes reported to camp authorities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we found ourselves in a situation, the clinic personnel, that we could not bear any more, all these stories, and we decided to do something. We had to do something, regardless of the risk, that we were exposing ourselves or those persons, and so we reported the rapes to Dr. Ivic and to the Commander of the camp. Dr. Ivic, most of all, organised that five girls who were raped be taken to the gynaecological department in the Prijedor hospital where they were checked. There was a doctor, also Serb, a female doctor, according to my information later, she was fired from her job. She was kicked out of the hospital because she protested over this. We were hopeful, we had great hope, that it would finally stop because everybody knew now what was going on, because now this is not an individual case and that they did not know. That is what we hoped. However, nothing went on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER CONTINUED
utterances.text: What was the effect of the occurrence of these rapes on the prisoners generally or the Muslim population generally, on their expectations, on their hopes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The very act of rape, in my opinion -- I spoke to these people, I observed their reactions -- it had a terribly negative effect on them. They could, perhaps, explain it to themselves when somebody steals somebody from them, or even beatings or even some killings. Somehow they sort of accepted it in some way, but when the rapes started they lost all hope. Until then they had hope that this war could pass, that everything would quiet down. When the rapes started everybody lost hope, everybody in the camp, men and women. There was such fear, horrible. They had fear from the night because at night there is a danger of being taken away again. One of them told me, I remember, "Are they going to come for me this night, tonight?" That is the question that is always there. They also knew of some of their neighbours, female neighbours, so they had terrible fear. My personal opinion is that one of the goals of that act was precisely to maintain this fear in the remainder of the Muslim population. That was the goal.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER CONTINUED
utterances.text: Sir, were you in camp on August 21st when a convoy left for Travnik via Vlasic Mountain?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, at that time I was at the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER CONTINUED
utterances.text: Was there anything different in the way this convoy was handled by Serb authorities than previous or later convoys?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was a great difference in the organisation of this convoy, namely, unlike the convoys that had left earlier, we knew a day before the departure that the convoy was being organised, that it was going the next day. Given that we had two cases, two inmates, that we were taking care of who had broken legs, who were brought back to us from the Prijedor hospital, we asked the Camp Commander to have these two patients released, to allow them to move, that they be moved because we could not help them. He allowed that. All the other prisoners knew about the departure. When the buses arrived, I think there was a small group of women who first got on to the bus, and I was also on it as an escort for my patients. When I got off the bus I saw two, two groups -- one group of persons in two columns who were waiting for this bus to arrive. They were all young people, younger people, between 30 and 50. I was very surprised because no men under 60 could leave the camp. Until then you could not mingle with women and children. It was strictly controlled. Of course, there were exceptions, in some ways individuals could buy their way out, but in this convoy they allowed them to get out. Moreover, behind the bus I saw a large column of people who were ready, who wanted to get on those buses. I was greatly surprised. I saw a guard who was almost pushing people inside so that more of them would fit. For us who were seeing all this, it was a big surprise that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER CONTINUED
utterances.text: So is it correct that in other convoys there were strict controls and it was extremely difficult and painstaking to get on, and in this case you saw guards virtually pushing people on to the buses to get them on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly, exactly. They even had problems to prevent them because there was not enough buses. Many wanted to get on when they saw that they had a possibility. That was the last chance for us. Many of them thought that was the last chance to leave. After that convoy, there were no more civilians. Everything was cleansed. Maybe one small group in one village, maybe five families left, but for us it was the last hope. So people went.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER CONTINUED
utterances.text: Did you later learn that this was the convoy from which many men were removed on Vlasic mountain and massacred?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The same day we heard on the radio -- we had a secret radio -- we heard that there was a massacre on the Vlasic Mountain, Mount Vlasic. Of course, other prisoners also heard about it. The next day, Major Kuruzovic, the Camp Commander, ordered that all prisoners assemble in the yard and he gave them a speech. He said that on Mount Vlasic only 20 people were killed, and that they were brought out or executed by a group of people who, sort of, as he put it, got out of control. But, later our information later, when we left the camp, I found out, we found out, that a large, large number of men from that convoy had been brought out and killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER CONTINUED
utterances.text: Was Major Kuruzovic interested in organising another convoy and was that effort blocked by the International Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, after that speech, the Major said to the people that there will be another convoy, that they should not be afraid to get into that convoy. Unfortunately, some believed him and waited for the buses for hours, but they never arrived. At that time the International Red Cross was already coming to the camp. They told us that we should not go in any convoys that have not been organised by the International Red Cross, and from there we would not go anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER CONTINUED
utterances.text: Sir, were you also in camp when prisoners who had been held in Omarska and Keraterm were transferred to Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, at that time I was also, and I remember very well that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER CONTINUED
utterances.text: Did you see them and treat some of them and, if so, what was their condition?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that day when they arrived, they appeared suddenly. Suddenly, there appeared buses who were coming in front of the entrance of our clinic where that main point was and then suddenly these people started coming out -- emaciated, unshaven, long hair, dirty, torn clothes. They were tatters practically, as we say. It was terrible. We were in the clinic and a soldier came and told us, "You don't have the right to leave". The entire perimeter has been additionally manned by soldiers and in columns, in twos, they were entering the perimeter of the camp, and they were in the field in front of the clinic and the movie theatre, and on the other side already the fence, the wire fence, was being put up so that the new arrivals would not be able to mix with the ones who were already there. Apart from this wire fence, there was security, the men were put. I was watching that and they were coming past me at about 13, 15 metres away, and it was tragic that I could not recognise almost anybody. They were very thin. What was characteristic was those eyes that looked big, sort of, protruding since the faces were sunken. I did not recognise my relatives, my good friends. I could not stand that after a while and I started moving slowly towards these people. Since I knew that guard, I tried to talk to them, and their voices were so weak I could barely hear them. I had to come closer and then some of them recognised me and they asked bread, they asked food, fruit. They were terribly, terribly hungry. One of them was lying on the staircase and said he had very strong pains in the leg. I asked the guard to take him to the clinic so that I could check on his leg and he allowed that. He let me. I took him. Somewhere around that time the International -- sorry -- the journalists from the western countries arrived so that other prisoners also said that they needed help, so that they just walked past that soldier and came over to us so that the hallway of our clinic was full of these people. We tried to help some of them. We were preparing tea for them so that they could have something to drink, so that they could, sort of, come to in a way.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER CONTINUED
utterances.text: Was this about the same time that the International Red Cross came to Trnopolje camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was August 4th -- I remember the date well -- and the International Red Cross was to arrive seven days later after that date, more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER CONTINUED
utterances.text: After the arrival of the International Red Cross, was there a change in the conditions within the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The circumstances changed radically as they brought us food, distributed it among the inmates. They brought medicines for our surgery which we needed urgently as we had many sick people. Furthermore, what was, perhaps, even more important than aid was to inmates was that they brought hope, hope that we might survive. Until that time, we did not know what would happen to us. We were afraid for our lives. But at that moment we trusted the International Red Cross immensely. We hoped that they would rescue us and get us out of that hell that we were living in. Also, our safety had much improved as we were put on record. However, it turned out later that that card did not mean safety by itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER CONTINUED
utterances.text: Did the International Red Cross organise a major convoy for prisoners to leave the camp scheduled for October 1st?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, on October 1st, the International Red Cross organised our evacuation from the camp. Prior to that, lists were compiled. Each of us was given a number, especially people who had to leave the camp. However, the Serb administration of the camp was making trouble and would not let us go, so that our departure was postponed for seven days. We should have left seven days earlier than we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER CONTINUED
utterances.text: Did the Serbian authorities place conditions on the departure of prisoners from Trnopolje camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, from conversations with representatives of the International Red Cross, they laid certain terms, namely, each one of us had to sign a statement in writing specifying that each one of us was leaving the territory of the Republika Srspka of his own free will, that he would never return with arms to that territory, or do anything against that state, as they put it, and that we were of our own free will making a present to them of all our movable and immovable property that we had. That was a condition. After that we were issued a paper, a statement, saying that we wanted to leave that territory and emigrate of our own will. Of course, we were forced to sign that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER CONTINUED
utterances.text: What was the initial reaction of the International Red Cross to the imposition of these conditions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the beginning, the International Red Cross was against our signing that, because that would be under duress. However, the camp administration conditioned on this the coming of the Red Cross. They said they would not allow them to come there or let us go out. In the end, they had to agree to us signing that. It was not easy to persuade people to sign that because nobody will give up his land of his own volition. That is something that he has been acquiring throughout his life.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER CONTINUED
utterances.text: Did the International Red Cross persuade people to do so by indicating the legitimacy or illegitimacy they thought these documents had?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they told us that we should sign that, nevertheless, because in this manner we would save our lives even though, legally speaking, that signature on that document had no legal validity, and that under the circumstances because it has been extorted because it was done under duress, and so people at long last agreed to sign those documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I have this document and its English translation marked as Exhibit 297 for identification, please? Sir, do you recognise this document or this Exhibit as being the document which you received from Serbian authorities after signing the relinquishment of property?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this is the document which I signed, like all my friends, on the day when we were leaving Trnopolje. Those who did not have such a document could not enter the bus, and this is the document we received two days before the departure.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER CONTINUED
utterances.text: Just to make it clear, this is not the relinquishment document but the document which you received after executing the relinquishment document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER CONTINUED
utterances.text: I would tender that for admission, your Honour, and ask that the English translation be placed briefly on the Elmo?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Exhibit 297 will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sir, without this document given by Serbian authorities, one could not be released from the camp, and one could not obtain this document without first agreeing that one was leaving the territory voluntarily and relinquishing all property voluntarily?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, quite so.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER CONTINUED
utterances.text: Sir, approximately two weeks before the convoy left, did a large number of people from outside the camp, Muslims from outside the camp, suddenly show up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, when it was learnt that we would be evacuated from Trnopolje, small trucks or vans began to arrive bringing individual families, complete families, from Prijedor, as a rule. Those were Muslims who had been promised that for about 500 marks, German marks, they would receive the card of the International Red Cross and by that very fact be able to leave that territory in that convoy which was leaving. At the outset, those were individual cases, one or two families, but day after day their number grew. As the day of our departure grew close, there were about 700 such people who were put in surrounding houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER CONTINUED
utterances.text: I am sorry, we did not get a clear translation of that. About how many people were there gathered from outside by the time of the convoy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 700 people altogether.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER CONTINUED
utterances.text: Was the International Red Cross reluctant to register these people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they only had the lists of us, of the inmates, and did not want to register them, their explanation being that in that manner they would be helping towards the ethnic cleansing of Prijedor and the surrounding area. They did not want to take part in that. They said that they had reached an agreement only on the departure of inmates, men, from Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER CONTINUED
utterances.text: What was the reaction of camp officials to the ICRC refusal or reluctance to register these people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They resisted it and said, "If you do not register those people too and take them away, not even the inmates will be able to leave the camp". So that there were very many problems between the Red Cross, on the one hand, and the camp administration on the other. It lasted for several days and after that a compromise was found. It was decided to register only 30 men. I do not know who had arrived in the camp, I do not know by which date, as they had also been registered by the Serb Red Cross upon their arrival. So there were about 30 men or so, and the women had to stay behind in the camp, having also been promised that the next convoy from Trnopolje would go within two weeks, within a fortnight.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER CONTINUED
utterances.text: Did those women leave Trnopolje camp within two weeks on another convoy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, all those people who had arrived and those who arrived subsequently stayed in the camp, and where, I do not know, but from what I know, from what I learnt later, they stayed there until early December of that same year, '92.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER CONTINUED
utterances.text: Was it just those people or did the numbers of people in the camp continue to grow after the departure of the main convoy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the arrival of people from Prijedor continued to grow, that is, their number continued to grow. They practically took our place in camp facilities. Around mid November, as far as I can remember, there were about 1500 of them. A person from the Red Cross paid us a visit in Karlovac at the time and told me that that was the figure that they had on their records.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER CONTINUED
utterances.text: On Thursday you mentioned that when you were taken first to the hospital in Prijedor and then to the Crisis Staff you were transported on a civilian bus?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Excuse me. We left by a civilian bus from Trnopolje to the clinic, to the hospital in Prijedor, and by that bus we also proceeded, we turned to the Crisis Staff because the driver refused to take us further.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER CONTINUED
utterances.text: Just to clarify, that is not a regular line bus but a bus that was used for camp purposes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, it was a bus placed at the disposal of the army which brought in guards or representatives of the Serb Red Cross to the Trnopolje camp, and there were no line buses and the driver had a uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER CONTINUED
utterances.text: Did it appear that military vehicles or, at least, many military vehicles had been diverted to areas where there were battles rather than in the area of Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, by the way, they did have a major problem with vehicles, with army vehicles. They appeared very seldom. They had been transferred to fronts, to other fronts, lines, so that many civilian trucks or buses or passenger cars had been engaged for military needs. Of course, the license plates had all been taken off or glued over, just a plaster or something, so that one could not read them. We knew it from conversations with those Serb guards that everything had gone to the front line, as they put it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER CONTINUED
utterances.text: Were prisoners who were taken from the camp and killed or who disappeared sometimes transported in civilian vehicles?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER CONTINUED
utterances.text: Would that be in both private cars and in trucks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, various means of transportation were used, depending on the number of people who were being taken away or the person coming in and asking for those inmates. Of course, if a larger group was being requested, then a larger vehicle would come. If smaller groups or individuals, then passenger cars would come. It also depended on people taking them out or asking them out. Those high ranking policemen came in luxury Mercedes cars, for instance, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER CONTINUED
utterances.text: Do you recall a day when six prisoners were taken from the camp in a civilian truck?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I do remember the incident, but the date or, rather, the time I could not fix more closely because, under the circumstances, the time had lost its import to us. We were trying to help people. We were endeavouring to provide medical care for them and we could not have cared less if it was Friday or Saturday or a Sunday. The time had stopped for us in a way. I remember -- I cannot remember the day when it happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER CONTINUED
utterances.text: To your knowledge, were those prisoners ever heard of or seen again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, those people were taken away in that small truck, and their fate or the fate of many others who were taken from the camp on subsequent occasions, we know nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER CONTINUED
utterances.text: Before the prisoners were taken from camp, had you seen that truck when it arrived in camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was in the surgery and I heard a sound. I looked through the window as I was by the window and I saw the truck arrive and park next to the road, partly next to the road, by the fence of those grounds in front of the surgery, around the surgery.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time if I could, perhaps, refer back to the previous Exhibit, not the immediately previous Exhibit, but Exhibit 296, the video, and that might help us identify the locations the witness is speaking about. If we could begin running Exhibit 296? I will ask our technicians to stop. Can we stop here for a moment? Sir, what is this building? I know you identified it previously.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this is the building which, in the front here, in the front of the picture, before the war it housed a coffee bar and during the war it was the headquarters of the Serb Red Cross and also the offices where the camp Commander, Major Kuruzovic, and Slavko Puhalic, his deputy head. In the back is the cinema where women with children were put.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER CONTINUED
utterances.text: Was the Serbian Red Cross housed in this building during the entire operation of the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, at a certain point it was here from the beginning of the camp until one day, I do not know the date, but it was moved to another office which was on the other side of the road, across this building. Before the war, it was also a restaurant, a pub.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER CONTINUED
utterances.text: Sir, I am going to ask that the tape be played forwards and if you can tell us to stop if you see the area where the truck parked when it arrived? Can we move forward now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER CONTINUED
utterances.text: Stop, please. I know you will be unable to point, but perhaps you can describe, using the land marks on the video, where the truck parked?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The truck was parked on the road more or less in parallel with that group of people that we can see on that picture there, next to the fence. Then come some shrubs, and this small truck was parked on the road. A group of people that we see beyond that lamp post, here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER CONTINUED
utterances.text: OK. From what direction had the truck come?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The truck arrived from the direction of Kozarac. Therefore, from the direction of the road that one can see in the background of this still, the direction of the mountain.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER CONTINUED
utterances.text: So the truck would have been, as we are looking at the video now, coming toward us and then parked on the side of the street closest ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER CONTINUED
utterances.text: --- to the building?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Tieger. If I understand the witness's testimony last Thursday, is this where the medical centre, for lack of a better word, was located?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. Can you tell us, sir, what the building we see in this picture is, the building by which these people are standing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The building that we see here served as a shop before the war, as a food store, and behind it to the left was where our surgery was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER CONTINUED
utterances.text: So the wall that we see moving toward the left side of the building is the area where the medical centre or ambulanta was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is right, and here between these two trees we see its window, we see our medical centre's window.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER CONTINUED
utterances.text: What kind of a truck was this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a small TAM truck. We called them TAM-ic, a small TAM. It had a canvas. So there was a cabin and the canvas in the back.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER CONTINUED
utterances.text: A sort of a canvas canopy over the back?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER CONTINUED
utterances.text: After it parked did you see anyone get out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I saw the driver who got off on the left. It was a uniformed soldier, but I could not see his face -- I could not identify him -- and he got off towards the road. I do not know where he headed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER CONTINUED
utterances.text: After a few minutes did you see someone in that area whom you recognised?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was standing by the window and continued to talk to my colleagues who were there, and then I cast another look on to the road and saw a group of soldiers standing by this main point on the road. It was a group of soldiers, uniformed men, separated from the group, and started towards the yard in front of the surgery, in front of the medical centre. After he had made a few steps, I recognised Dusan Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER CONTINUED
utterances.text: The group of soldiers that you saw, can we see the approximate position where they were on the video as it is now on the screen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were on the road to the right of the screen where this darkish part is, this, how shall I put it, the lower third slightly beyond the middle of the screen, if I can orient it like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER CONTINUED
utterances.text: Then one of the uniformed men separated from the group and began to walk in the direction of the ambulanta?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER CONTINUED
utterances.text: After he left the group and as he approached the ambulanta, you realised it was Dule Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER CONTINUED
utterances.text: Where did he go after he left the group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He started towards the entrance, through the gate towards the yard in front of our medical centre, and then continued towards the building housing the Serb Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER CONTINUED
utterances.text: Can we roll the tape backwards just a little bit, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Before you do that ---

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I am sorry, can we stop? Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I did not follow the ----

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: My microphone light will not come on. Is the microphone working now? No, none of them are.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: There is a green blinking light by Judge Vohrah's and perhaps by yours as well -- if that will help for us to determine what may be the cause.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I did not follow the reference to the dark patch on the road. I saw a dark patch on the road, but it is very long and I do not know where he is describing the group of soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can we role the tape forward slightly to the position it was previously? Can we keep going a bit? OK. Sir, I know it is difficult to describe this in words rather than simply pointing, but if I can ask you to make another attempt at indicating to us where that checkpoint was and where the group of soldiers were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If we watch the bottom half of the right portion of the screen, you can see the road separating to the right. That is the entrance to the house that was there. About three or four metres below this entrance was where the soldiers were. I think you can see a dark spot and, like, a pot hole damaged roadway. This is where they were, approximately. That means in the part where the white portion of the asphalt is going to the right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, would this be an appropriate time?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, is your microphone not working as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It is now, but it has not been all morning.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We will stand in recess then for 20 minutes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I believe there was a delay occasioned by the need to set up some technical equipment. Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, thank you. I apologise for the delay. I recognised prior to today that the description that the witness is now involved in would be facilitated by a series of still photographs to which he could point on the Elmo. We have temporarily -- I trust only temporarily -- lost the capacity to do that. I earlier enquired of the technical people here in court whether that was possible and was told it was not. During the break we believed there was the opportunity to extract some quick stills. That attempt was made but was unsuccessful. So we will try to struggle along as we have been doing through words rather than still shots to which we can point.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Do you have additional copies of the photos or, at least, one for the Bench that we could use and one for the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No. I was unable to even to attempt to make such stills prior to the break.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: From the video?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That is right. The frames which we attempted to extract during the break, the quality simply was not high enough so that I think it will be of any meaningful use.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We will follow the witness's best attempt -- are you ready to proceed?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Very good. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If we could before we begin return to the portion of the video which was on screen just before we adjourned, just before we recessed. Thank you. [To the witness]: Once again, sir, where was it that you saw Dule Tadic go after he left the group and walked in the direction of the clinic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic separated from the group and walked towards the entrance to the yard which is across from the clinic, that is, towards the trees that you can -- that can be seen here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER CONTINUED
utterances.text: Then where did he go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He went into the building in which the Serbian Red Cross was located.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER CONTINUED
utterances.text: Can we roll the video backwards a bit? Stop there, please? In this portion of the video, sir, can we see both the building into which Mr. Tadic went and also see a portion of the ambulanta and one of the windows of the ambulanta?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, on the left we see the large white building, that is, the building where the Red Cross was housed. In the right, on the right side of the screen, we see the building with windows and the window we see is the window of the ambulanta.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER CONTINUED
utterances.text: After Mr. Tadic entered the building to the left where the Serbian Red Cross premises were, did you remain in the same room from which you had seen him go into the building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I was called by a patient who entered the room that we used for check-ups and I went to that room to see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER CONTINUED
utterances.text: Was there also a window in that room?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER CONTINUED
utterances.text: Is that, essentially, adjacent to the window we see in the photograph and in roughly the same part of the building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Those were the rooms next to one another.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER CONTINUED
utterances.text: Did you see Mr. Tadic come out of the building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, when I walked into that room I saw through this other window as Mr. Tadic -- as Mr. Tadic was walking out of the building of the Red Cross and returning to the group of soldiers which was still standing on the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER CONTINUED
utterances.text: About how long was that after he had entered the building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very short, a very short time, a minute or two.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER CONTINUED
utterances.text: Did you continue to watch?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was still watching him when he came back to the group of people and he was talking to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER CONTINUED
utterances.text: How long did he remain with that group of soldiers or persons in uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Also very short, a minute at the most.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER CONTINUED
utterances.text: Where did he go then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After that he again went back to the premises of the Red Cross the same way.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER CONTINUED
utterances.text: Did you see him come out of the premises of the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER CONTINUED
utterances.text: About how long after he entered this time was it that he came out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He also stayed there a very -- for a very short time. He came out also one to two minutes, very quick, it was all very quick, but this time he walked out together with the Deputy Commander, Slavko Puhalic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER CONTINUED
utterances.text: In which direction did they start to go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They walked out of this building and, after about three or four metres in front of this staircase that we see, they stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER CONTINUED
utterances.text: What were they doing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic gave a piece of paper to Slavko who then read it, looked at it, that piece of paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER CONTINUED
utterances.text: About how far away from your position at the window were they at this time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were some 12, 13 metres away from me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER CONTINUED
utterances.text: Were they positioned roughly to the right of the window, to the left of the window, or just straight ahead of the window as you were watching?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were approximately in the direction of where I was looking, by the window.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER CONTINUED
utterances.text: What was happening as they talked?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic was pointing his finger on the paper that Slavko was holding in his hand. He was asking him something -- I do not know exactly, I could not hear it clearly -- Slavko was responding, but the topic of their conversation was that paper, that list. The conversation was short in terms of questions and answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER CONTINUED
utterances.text: From where you were watching, could you make out the words on the paper?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course I could not see what was written on that paper. I could not see what was written, the words, but in that moment I saw that the right side was blank, was unwritten, and the left side was written out, like a column.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER CONTINUED
utterances.text: Had you seen papers written in that fashion before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, before I saw them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER CONTINUED
utterances.text: When had you seen papers written with a column down one side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On one occasion Slavko Puhalic came to us in the clinic, in the room where we, sort of, used as a rest, to rest. At one point he produced a piece of paper out of his pocket and I was next to him at that time. He said, "I am interested in something, do you know these people?" He started reading names of people from Kozarac that we knew. He asked us where they were now, whether we knew where they were and whether we knew anything about them. I saw clearly the names of -- some names of those people.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER CONTINUED
utterances.text: Those were names of Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, those were names of Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER CONTINUED
utterances.text: Were any of those persons located or found by Deputy Commander Puhalic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We said that we did not know anybody, that we did not know where they were at that moment, we just did not know. He said that, he asked us to try to remember whether we knew anything about them and we said we did not. After that he again took his paper and kept it in his hand and folded it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER CONTINUED
utterances.text: Do you know whether or not any of those persons he was looking for were eventually located?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When he left us he went to the perimeter of the camp and there they had some kind of roll calls. That happened often in the camp. When they were looking for somebody, they asked that all the inmates would gather in the yard in front of the school and line up in columns. Then they had to come to the part where the Serb policemen or soldiers were checking their identity. Everybody had to show their licna karta or some personal ID. If their name was on the list that they had, they would be separated from the rest. On that day they found two from that list.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER CONTINUED
utterances.text: What happened to those two who were found?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They brought them to the premises of that commune centre near the ambulanta and there they interrogated and beat them. After that beating they brought them past our windows and locked them up in the lab which they used as a prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER CONTINUED
utterances.text: Did those prisoners remain there or did they eventually disappear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the afternoon of that day, those two were taken in a private vehicle and they disappeared. We never heard from them again.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER CONTINUED
utterances.text: Getting back to the occasion you were describing for us, did Dule Tadic and Slavko Puhalic remain in that courtyard area discussing that piece of paper and pointing to that piece of paper for a period of time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Slavko held that paper and read from it. They talked briefly, and at one moment Slavko said something, I do not know what, but then Dule -- something upset Mr. Tadic. He was excited. He was nervous. He started moving around him. They kept talking with their voices a bit raised, and that went on for about five minutes. Then both of them again went towards the entrance, to the gate, to the group of soldiers that were still standing in the street, on the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER CONTINUED
utterances.text: As Dule Tadic and Slavko Puhalic went to that group in the road, did you see any other persons approaching the group whom you recognised?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When they started from that spot where they had stopped, I was watching them and that moment I saw on the road below the group of soldiers that was, there two persons that I recognised.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER CONTINUED
utterances.text: Who were they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was Miso Radulovic and then next to him was a soldier from the guard and on the right-hand side was Goran Borovnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER CONTINUED
utterances.text: How were Miso Radulovic and Goran Borovnica dressed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Miso Radulovic and Goran Borovnica were dressed in olive green uniforms of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER CONTINUED
utterances.text: Did you know Miso Radulovic and Goran Borovnica before the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I knew them both.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER CONTINUED
utterances.text: How did you know Miso Radulovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Miso Radulovic was a teacher in the primary school, Rade Kondic, in Kozarac to which I went for eight years. I often saw him in the school, in the school building.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER CONTINUED
utterances.text: How did you know Goran Borovnica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Borovnica is a year younger than I am and he went to the same class with a relative of mine. I knew him from the playground, from the soccer field, and later Goran worked in a restaurant, Crvene Ruze, as a waiter that I patronised often at that time and in a cafe owned by Mr. Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER CONTINUED
utterances.text: Did Borovnica have anything unusual or distinctive about his appearance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Borovnica had a handicap. Actually, his strabism he had -- his eyes were cross-eyed. That was very characteristic of him. It is something that is very conspicuous.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER CONTINUED
utterances.text: I do not mean to get technical. Was it the kind of condition where both eyes were focused inward or one eye would focus in one direction and the other eye would focus inward?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is exactly it.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Which one?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Which one? The latter? The second? One eye would focus in one direction and one eye would focus inward, is that it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One eye practically -- there are two types of this condition. One is fixating on an object, but the other one is not following that but is going in another direction. So one is looking straight and one is looking inward, that is one of the possibilities, and that is strabism.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER CONTINUED
utterances.text: I asked what you Goran Borovnica and Miso Radulovic were wearing. Do you recall what Dule Tadic was wearing on that date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dusan Tadic wore a camouflage uniform that was worn by some other Serbian soldiers. It is a camouflage military uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER CONTINUED
utterances.text: Did Goran Borovnica and Miso Radulovic also go to the group of soldiers at the checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were moving in the direction of this group. Then they joined it very soon. They were joined by Tadic and Slavko and then they continued to talk.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER CONTINUED
utterances.text: After that what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: By being, by observing so long, I had been away from the patient for quite a while, so then I turned back to him and continued the treatment practically.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: At this time can we take the second video clip which is very short which may help us in lieu of photographs? I would like that tendered as 298 for identification, not tendered but at least marked. Can we stop, please? Can we move that back slightly? Thank you. Sir, is this another shot of the building which Dule Tadic entered and from which deputy Commander Puhalic and Mr. Tadic emerged?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER CONTINUED
utterances.text: Does it show the general area where they were standing and talking about the paper?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the place where they were standing is in front of the building, some three or four metres away from those stairs. On the screen, we see that in the direction of this middle arch. On the pavement there is a white stone, and that is where they were at that moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER CONTINUED
utterances.text: Can we roll it forward, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER CONTINUED
utterances.text: If we can continue forward? Stop. Does this show the wall of the ambulanta which was partially obscured in the portions of the video we saw before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, quite right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER CONTINUED
utterances.text: Does it show the windows from which you were able to observe what was happening?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, on the window which is to the right of the screen and that is the window through which I looked the first time when I recognised Mr. Tadic, and to the left, and that is the other window which is to the left, is the window which was in this examination room that we had and through which I watched Dusko Tadic and Puhalic discussing the list which Slavko held in his hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Could I ask a question?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: The window to the right that we are looking at that there, do you say that that is the same window as we could see through the trees in the earlier photograph which also showed the road?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, on that film we saw the third window which is even further to the right, as compared with this window. There is yet another window which is to the right of this one shown here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would tender 298 for admission.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No objection, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: 298 will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sir, do you see Dule Tadic in court today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER CONTINUED
utterances.text: Can you point him out and tell us what he is wearing, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic is sitting in the back of the room. He has a jacket, a suit with a light blue shirt and a tie.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: May the record reflect the identification of the accused, your Honour?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes, the record will reflect that the witness identified the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I have nothing further. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Cross-examination, Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. Before I start cross-examination, might the technical booth provide us with Exhibit 296 on the video monitor, that portion of the road that we have been observing?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, if we could just hold it on there? Mr. Gutic, the first matter I want to ask you about is this. You are unable to help us with any date that you say that you saw Mr. Tadic here at Trnopolje, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, unfortunately. Should I explain?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You gave a reason earlier when you were giving evidence for the Prosecution. Is there anything extra that you need to tell us about that that is different from what you have told us before? Can you tell us when you left Trnopolje? How long did you stay there for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Trnopolje I spent, I was from 26th May '92 to 1st October '92, I spent at Trnopolje camp all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You have told us about people coming to the camp and sometimes people leaving. It was also the case that certain families left the camp to go and live elsewhere in the region. Families were able to move from there, for instance, and go and live in Prijedor. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a possibility during the early days when the camp was formed. The camp grounds were overcrowded, so that at some point the camp administration allowed, I think it was, two buses with women and children to leave the camp, under the condition, though, that they had some relatives or friends who could look after them, but that was an exception. In other words, those were people under that condition and a very limited number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Presumably, there was some kind of documentation that had to be prepared to enable people to live elsewhere other than the camp, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not quite understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were you aware, for instance, if any documents had to be prepared to enable these people to live elsewhere, for instance in Prijedor, rather than remain in the camp itself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One needed a certificate of the Serb Red Cross. Only those who had that certificate could leave the camp and go to Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Some families were taken from the camp to live in the villages around Trnopolje, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, women with small children were allowed to leave the camp grounds and be accommodated in houses which were adjoining the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, the camp itself, as you have described it, also included houses in the surrounding area of Trnopolje where a number of families were billeted, so it was not just the confines of that area around the school and the cinema. A number of the surrounding houses also contained families who were under the control of Trnopolje camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, a couple of houses adjacent to the camp, adjoining the fence of the camp, were also used to accommodate where our inmates lived, but there were also houses on the other side of the road and which were used by Serb soldiers for their own needs and they picked out those that suited them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were you familiar with the documents that were used to enable people to be discharged from the camp and live elsewhere? Did you see those documents yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were they officially prepared documents, typed, printed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were typed. It was a small piece of paper typed on a typewriter, and the space for their name was left empty, and there the name of the person who had the possibility of leaving was entered at that moment. But that was immediately after the camp was set up. It was during that period of time, that is, the first 15 days. That is when those certificates were issued. They were signed by Major Kuruzovic or Pero Curguz, as the head of the Serb Red Cross, and they brought a seal of the municipality of Prijedor, the old seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you know if those documents were prepared and produced in the camp offices at Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, it said "potvrda", certificate, but it could also be used in other institutions before the war. It did not have any specific purpose, these documents, these certificates. For instance, those girls who worked in the Red Cross had them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: They were documents that were actually prepared in, perhaps, Kuruzovic's office or the office of the Deputy Commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were written in the office of the Serb Red Cross and that person had to take it to Major Kuruzovic for signature or later on to Pero Curguz, as I have just said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When any of the detainees at the camp was required to go elsewhere, perhaps to look for food and had a release from the camp, would that detainee be provided with some sort of document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These documents were issued only to women and children and, as for the inmates, those who went in search of food, they were not issued any certificates. They simply had to leave their personal documents at the checkpoint. Later on, when people from Omarska and Keraterm arrived, it was made possible for a small -- for a specified number that on the basis of a very bad state of health but that also had to be documented, they also had the possibility of leaving the camp and going to Prijedor, provided they were from Prijedor and had a house, some accommodation, a dwelling, in Prijedor. Presumably, there were some other conditions but I do not know about them. I know only what I heard from those people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were there any certificates at all for a temporary discharge from the camp to show that the person could leave Trnopolje and, perhaps, go to his home village and there look for food or return with food to the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that our inmates -- that to obtain food our inmates did not need those certificates. They were not issued to them. Personally, I did get a certificate, a piece of paper, I have to tell you, from Mr. Kuruzovic so that I could go to a nearby village and try to find milk for infants and possibly some food. That was on one occasion. I said that was an exception.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: But other people may have been able to use certificates in such way for themselves? You say yours was an exception, but others may have also had such certificates to enable them to move elsewhere on a temporary basis?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Turning to this occasion now when you have described the lorry or truck arriving at the camp and parking on the side of the road. If we could just have that picture again from Exhibit 296 on our screen? Thank you. Just to indicate to us because we have had nothing able to be marked, in relation to that telegraph pole quite near the building -- can you see that -- where in relation to that did the truck park?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The truck was parked behind it, that is, towards that group of people we see here in the central part of the still and parallel with them on the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They are next to the fence itself and the truck was on the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You saw one man get out of the truck?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw only the driver get off.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you know where he went?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He got off the truck and I did not see him again. He went somewhere, I do not know where he went, but he did not join that group of soldiers standing there on the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You did not see any soldiers getting out of the back of the truck?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The rear part, I could see the truck up to the edge, but then I could not see the end of it because there was the corner of the building which hid it from my view. So I do not know whether anybody got off.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It seems then that the group of soldiers you indicated, you suddenly noticed? You do not know where they came from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That place where those soldiers were standing was otherwise the chief point of the camp where the guard Commander -- excuse me, the shift Commander of those guards who were then on duty and four or five soldiers standing sentry at that point. So that was the chief place where those who would come to the camp grounds had to apply. So, that was the point which was permanent, which was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So the position that you indicated the soldiers were in, was a checkpoint or guard point for the camp, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The entrance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That point was on the road, you indicated to us, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was -- there is a building, a former private restaurant was there with a roof and with a marquee and the soldiers were spending time next to the -- in the shadow, in the shade, of that restaurant or around that part. They moved. They moved about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So if we had looked to the right of that photograph not shown on our screen, there was a building that the guards used as their headquarters or base for the camp, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there is an overhanging roof there and the private house which housed a former restaurant before the war. Right next to the road there is a small fence and then the entrance into that building.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did those guards control the access of people into the camp and the people leaving the camp from that position in the road that you indicated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If a vehicle arrived from the direction of Kozarac, it would be halted at that northern most point and would be controlled there. Then it would be sent to this central point where the shift Commander was and in those rooms next to it, that is, in that house Major Kuruzovic subsequently moved in. That is where the Red Cross offices were. So, if a truck or any other vehicle came from the direction of Prijedor, it would also be halted on the road and then it would proceed to that particular point so that was the central point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your evidence was that after this truck arrived, a few minutes later you recognised a soldier amongst that group whom you say was Dusko Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I have said, when the truck parked, when it stopped, I turned towards the interior of the room in which I was and I was talking to an individual and then later on, a couple of minutes later, I again turned towards the road, that is, I looked outside and I saw that group of soldiers which was now larger. At that moment, immediately after that, one of them turned and started for the entrance into the yard in front of the surgery and I recognised him then as Mr. Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So the answer to my question was yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I have said, the soldier who split from the group moved towards the surgery, I recognised him and that was Dusko Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I would like you to look at this photograph which I tender as Exhibit -- no, it will be Defence Exhibit 28, I believe, your Honour. If you could look at it, Mr. Gutic, and then put it on the monitor for us? Can you show it to Mr. Tieger? That is a photograph there, Mr. Gutic, of the front of the building that housed the Serbian Red Cross, and the camp Commander's officers as well as the cinema that was behind, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: On the right-hand side you can see part of the front of the shop building that was at the front of the ambulanta where you were positioned during your observation of this road, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but you cannot see ambulanta from here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, but we can see the general area. If you could put that on the monitor for us, Mr. Bos, and we can switch on our computer monitors? Thank you. What I am interested in, Mr. Gutic, is how you claim from that position in the ambulanta to be able to see a list of names across that yard being held by Mr. Tadic or the Deputy Commander in front of the Red Cross building. What distance are we talking about from your place inside the ambulanta to that area where the white stone was that you indicated in front of the arch to the building? How many metres would you say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said, and that is how it was, the distance from the window by which I stood to the place where Tadic was standing was about 12 or 13 metres. Of course, I never measured it, but that is roughly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: They were placed facing you or sideways to you when you were looking from your window or did they have their backs to you? How were they placed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the moment when they were standing, Slavko Puhalic had his left profile to me and Mr. Tadic was to his right, and when they stopped, when they stopped, Tadic turned his face towards me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Who was holding the document that you say was a list?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When they came out of the Red Cross office and came down those stairs, Mr. Tadic then handed over that list to Slavko, turned or made another step and then they stopped. Slavko was holding the list in his hands at that moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So were you looking at the piece of paper sideways on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You say from that position you were able to observe that there was a list of names, do you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that the right side of that sheet was white, and one could see it clearly. There was a difference between the written part which was to the left, from top to the bottom, and the right-hand side which was white which had not been used.
