utterances.text: Before the war, no, I did not notice that he was active in politics. But when the Serb authority took over in Prijedor and, what do I know, then or rather earlier before that, towards the end of April, television and all the rest were cut off, that is, the television in Sarajevo. All one could watch was television Belgrade and once -- I did not believe that he could be a member of some Party, I do not know, of some national, some Serb Party, but then I watched a report from Prijedor, from a session, and he was siting there also amongst those authorities of theirs that they had brought. Later on I learned that there were those whom I saw and it was not really particularly laudable.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you yourself interested in politics?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, never in my life was I active in politics, nor did I know what it was. I worked day and night because I was a poor man, so I wanted to create something and had two sons -- as a matter of fact, I still have two sons and a daughter -- so that I worked. Sometimes, when need be, I was also an upholsterer and sometimes, so as to keep my word, I worked throughout the night.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In addition to what you saw on television, did you ever read or hear about an article written about Dusko Tadic in the newspaper concerning a letter that he is said to have received?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Several papers wrote about it, but I do not know whether it was Glas of Banja Luka or a Prijedor paper or Kozarski Vjesnik wrote about those letters, saying that a group of, what do I know, perhaps not a group, but some younger Muslims had sent him a letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know what the nature of this letter was that was sent to him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not, I mean, I could not really guess. Some said it was political reasons, others said it was commercial reasons. Then one of the journalists said, "If you do not hate Muslims, Dusko Tadic, please prove that. Open your coffee bar to see what was there".

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: But I am asking you, Mr. Jakupovic, if you can tell us what the letter was about, did you know, not the reasons for being sent but what it was about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What do you mean? I do not understand. In that story, in that story in the papers or in the letter?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, the story you read in the paper, what did it say the letter was about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, they said, I do not remember the title, but it was an ugly title for those people in Kozarac. It said that Dusko Tadic had received a threatening letter, that he, his wife, his children, what do I know, would be killed, I do not remember the contents, and then the signature was mladi Muslimani -- young Muslims -- from Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know whether this was subsequently investigated, this letter that had been sent?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard from some young men, some were even summoned, those who were suspected, but nobody was discovered, the authors of this letter from what I heard and I knew nothing about it until about, I do not know, until about some months ago. I bought a book issued by a television cameraman from Sarajevo and ----

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You need not tell us about what you read a couple of months ago. I just wanted you to tell us what you knew at the time. Did you ever go or have occasion to go into the cafe bar of Dusko Tadic, the Nipon cafe bar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I frequented it. My son worked there for a while and I went even after that letter because after all I was a next door neighbour, and other people whom I considered cleverer than I was and others thought that we should frequent it as much as possible because others boycotted it and did not go.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Why did you do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was his next door neighbour, so as to somehow combat the evil. Simply, I was a Muslim and if this letter was sent, then perhaps he could think that it had been written in my house or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You said earlier in your evidence that you and your family had moved to Prijedor where you stayed for a period of some four months. During the time that you were in Prijedor, did you ever see Dusko Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: On how many occasions did you see him in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When, approximately, as best you can remember, was the first time that you saw him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know exactly. I cannot say the month. I think it was in August. I was gathering some documentation for emigration because for two and a half months I had not stepped outside. I was not seen by the sun or the moon, as the saying goes. Then I decided to ask for that and to leave, if I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you hear that people were able to get papers which permitted them to leave the Prijedor area and go outside of Yugoslavia or, I should add, Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What was required of people in order to do this? What did they have to do in order to gain these papers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One needed previously, I think, 12 or 13 different certificates that you paid up all your phone bills, your utility bills, that you were not in debt with banks, a lot of things, but one of the main ones was from SUP. It was taken at SUP and that was a certificate about no previous criminal record and the men would go and then also the cessation of residence, and I gathered some of these documents, in fact my wife did too, but when I needed this cessation of residence certificate, I could not go there, I did not dare. I heard there were long lines and if there was a man on the line the police would come and take him away.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So did you seek the assistance of your brother-in-law in relation to this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was not far from me, but we did not see each other. We did not dare go out. There was the police curfew all the time and, in general, you could not go out. We talked on the phone, and he said that we should ask for this certificate and I said I dare not go. He says that Dule could do this, and he arranged with him so that he would come to me and that I would go with him to take out this certificate.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When he said "Dule would do this", by whom did you understand "Dule" to mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I know that -- I knew that he did it for him too.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No. I am asking you whom did you understand "Dule" to be, Dule who?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dusko Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you then go to the SUP building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was arranged that we meet in front of a state run pub and we met there and we went.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you say "we met there", tell us who it was in the party, each member of the party you met?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dusko and myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was your brother-in-law there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you met Dusko Tadic, did you have a conversation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, just on the way he asked me, "Where were you up until now? Where are your children? Everybody alive?" things like that. Meanwhile, we arrived at the SUP and passed by a huge crowd of people in the line and got inside.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you with Dusko Tadic all the time as you passed this long line?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, yes, I came with him to the door of that office where the certificates were being taken out. There was a long line, one to the next, and he went over to this clerk and he got the certificate and we met in the hallway in front at the entrance.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When he gave the certificate to you, did he say anything to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When he gave me the certificate he said, "I have to tell you something. It is all in vain, these documents that you are chasing". I saw, I do not know where, he saw the list for people to be arrested and I was on that list.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What did you say to him then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that I could not believe that, that if there was anybody who was innocent, who was not guilty at all, that was me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What did he say to you then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He asked me, "You worked on a wholesale warehouse, were you sending any food for this TO which was in Kozarac?" and I said "No", that that was a computer database and you could not, even the director could not take out any chocolate. It was well organised and strictly controlled, but it did not even occur to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: By the "TO" did you understand him to mean the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What did you say to him then? What happened then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I asked him, what should I do?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What did he say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He said, "I do not know" or "What do you want?" and I said, "Can you verify this?" I do not believe it because my name, as far as I know, on the census there were about 7,000 of my people with my last name. Then right there we went to another office. I think -- I do not think that even the door was closed to that office. He walked inside and I stood about two, three metres away from there, and a large strong man came. He was an officer, a police officer. I do not know what his rank was. He asked, "What is the matter?"

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did Dule Tadic say something to him, to this big officer that you saw, the tall officer that came?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He told him -- I do not know how you are going to understand me; it was, it was as a joke -- "I caught my neighbour", and he used the word "uhitio" which is a Croatian word for "to catch".

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Who said that? Who said, "I caught my neighbour"? Was that Dusko Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dusko, yes, laughing, he said to the officer. He saw that that was not it, so he said again, "What's the matter?" Then he said, "I read that he is on the list for people to be arrested. He is my neighbour and he would like to verify that he does not believe it."

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What happened then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then the officer called some man, a policeman who was thin and tall. He went upstairs and after about four or five minutes he returned. He said, "Yes, he is on the list but not on the main one." Then he said "Yes". I do not know if he said he was not in the main book or on the main list. What he said was, "He is on the list but not the main one."

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What did he say to you then after this? What did the officer then say to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then this one said, "OK, it doesn't matter, you can go. If we need you we will find you."

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: After you stayed in Prijedor for that four-month period, where did you go then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After four months we were in the house of a man who worked in Germany, and a friend of my wife put us up there and there was food there. That was then and then the food ran out. There were problems at night and day time. Then we heard that there was a rescue in Trnopolje, that the Red Cross would bring people out who went there. So we decided to go to Trnopolje camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you said "bring people out", did you understand that to mean taking people out of Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So, did you and your family then go to Trnopolje camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was this on 2nd October 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you arrived at Trnopolje camp, can you tell the Court what the conditions of the camp were like on 2nd October 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Who was weak of heart they could have had a heart seizure. Next to the school building they built large holes and these provisional toilets were made, and then around the toilets there were faeces, maybe 20 metres, maybe farther out, huge piles of crockery, of clothes, other things, on the other side tents. It was terrible. When you entered you were shocked.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What was the situation with respect to the water supply there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a truck -- before we arrived, myself and my family, it was put there by the International Red Cross. I do not know if there was something plastic there. There was water and then you came and you stood in line. They said that the water was not drinkable, so there were two pumps across the street, two just hand pumps for water.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where were you and your family located in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My son was on the staircase where they were put in like a janitors' room, that is where he was with a couple of his friends his age, and then the younger son with his then girlfriend (they are married now and they were separated). My wife was in a classroom. It was considered secure, it was four or five in. I was in the boiler room.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was this all in the school building itself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The school building was packed. There was an old building at the end of that perimeter that was for building materials and it was full. There was an old agricultural commune building, I do not know if you know what that is. Then there was a cinema theatre. That is how it was built. There were other buildings. There was a clinic and then there was a store and that was full too. In the back behind the school, that is between the school and the cinema theatre, there was something like a playground where they would put up tents from armoured wire, and then over that was put whatever, plastic paper, whatever they found. It was better under those tents than inside because the sewer broke inside and then all the faeces were coming out, and then they separated it out with blankets and other clothes. Then halfway down the hallway the children were lying because there was no room anywhere else, and so they had to make a choice. They were too cold, so there was nowhere else to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Approximately how many people were located in these various buildings and in the plastic makeshift tents that you have described?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They say there were about 3500 people. It was on a day when Mazowiecki came. That is what I heard. When he came, when he saw it he was crying like a child. That is when I heard from the interpreter that there were 3500 people there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was the camp guarded? Were the prisoners in the camp under guard?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you first arrived there did you know where the guards had come from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I arrived I did not know, but I heard right away after about half an hour that those were the native villagers from Trnopolje which frightened me. There was the last name Cavic, a short stocky, I think shorter than I am, he was the worst that they said. They told, "Don't come near him for anything in the world."

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did the guards subsequently change? Did they change the guards after you had arrived there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Later they changed the guards when the International Red Cross arrived, and then some professor, I do not know what his name is, and a doctor was also there. They talked to us and talked about the conditions, and then they were coming in with little flash lights, would take good shoes if they found any in front of the doors. They were taking young girls. Then after a few days the guards changed. They put real policemen, younger men, dressed uniformly and they were correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: These younger men that were recruited as the guards, do you know what nationality they were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not know. They were speaking Serbian language. They probably were Serbs. I think theoretically otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know where they come from, what part of Yugoslavia they had come from these new guards that came in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that they could have been from Prijedor. I was almost all over Yugoslavia, in Yugoslavia and abroad, and I knew the dialects, I knew the Serbo-Croat dialect. I think most probably they were all from Prijedor or surrounding areas or maybe Banja Luka. I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: But you were not sure precisely from what area from their accents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not. I was not leaving the building without some important, you know, if you went to get bread or something.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So are you saying that you stayed in the building most of the time unless you absolutely had to go out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you speak to the guards from time to time or did you avoid this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I never spoke to anybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When these guards changed from the old guards to the new ones that were brought in, about when did that happen, can you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know, I mean date-wise I do not, but maybe half a month after we arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How were these people dressed, these guards dressed, the new guards that came?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were dressed in camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were they armed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What sorts of arms did they carry?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Pistols for the most part and rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What was the main colour of the uniform, the camouflage uniform they wore?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That camouflage uniform was multi-coloured. It was camouflage. I do not know about the colours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were prisoners who were kept in the camp permitted to leave the camp at any time, or was there some special arrangement for this to occur?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not go until that last December 2nd when I first came out. Maybe some people went if they knew somebody. The money was essential. You could go if you had money. So that one of those, one of the guards or somebody who came in whom they knew from the soldiers, from Serbs, would give him a lift. Personally I do not know. I did not have where to go or business to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What was the population of the prisoners made up of mostly in terms of sex and age?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry, I did not quite get it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What was the population of the prisoners of the camp made up of mostly in terms of sex and age?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were all ages from infants who were -- they were just saying that an elderly man died from old age over there in the gymnasium, but for the most part women, children, elderly and some youth.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were there many men of military age there and by that I mean from 16 to 55 kept in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were, but those were for the most part those who were in the Omarska camp, the Manjaca camp and when they came back, when they got out, I do not know if they had a connection or something and were in Prijedor, were not in Trnopolje when the International Red Cross came and took away all the inmates. Then there were those who managed to survive like myself, my sons and others, but very few young ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: While you were in the camp were prisoners taken out by the guards from time to time that you could see?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not see.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you ever hear of this happening?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, when we first arrived, the first day the men were, you were pretending that you are invisible, false, so that you would not be noticed. They were just taken out and killed and I said, "How do you mean?" There were guards. I said, of course, but there all these gardens filled with dead bodies. They were all taken out and killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: While you were in the camp did you on any occasion see Dusko Tadic at the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When was it that you saw him in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The precise date I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Can you give us an approximate date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think somewhere when I came, maybe 10 days later, somewhere around there. I know that it had already started to rain.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where were you on this day that he came to the camp, where were you located at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was in a classroom where I was sleeping at the time. It was a cabinet for the physics.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: An acquaintance of mine came in and was a bit upset and he said, "Down on the road there's Dusko Tadic, he is looking for you." I said "Really?" He said "really." I went. I did not talk to my family or anything. I went down to the road and, indeed, there he was with another man whom I did not know until then.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you go up to Dusko Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was standing on the road when I came out of the school, and since it was raining we went and stood under a roof. He said, "I brought this man. He saw your house," he says. In fact this man introduced himself right away and he said his name, I do not remember it, but I think he told me his name and he said: "I am from Kladusa." I said: "Are you really from Kladusa itself?" I do not know if it is from Kladusa or a village next to it. He said: "I live there. I have a house with a top floor. Why don't we swap? If you cannot go back to your house, I can go to your house so that you do not get a barn for a house." For me that was such a notion not to go back. It is not nice to say, but I really thought that when that war start today it would last for one day. So he said: "Well, let me see if I survive. If I survive then we can make a deal."

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: This man whom you say came from Kladusa, is that also known as Velika Kladusa?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Velika Kladusa. I was never in Velika Kladusa. I also heard that there was a Mala Kladusa. I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: This man that was with Dusko Tadic, did you understand why it was that he was in Kozarac at this particular point in time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not know. He told me that he was also driven out or that he escaped from there, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you understand him to be a refugee from Velika Kladusa?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know what nationality he was, this man that spoke to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: While you were in the camp did you understand that there were a number of refugees from the Velika Kladusa area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not know that. When I came to the camp from Prijedor I did not budge from there until I went back to Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: But did you subsequently find this out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I found it out later, that from Kladusa, that part between Trnopolje and Kozarac, that it was taken, but part of it was not destroyed by Papuca.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, we will adjourn until tomorrow at 10 a.m. (5.30 p.m.). (The court adjourned until the following day).
